speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITIONS OF LANDS TO ESTABLISH GREEN BELT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement at this time regarding the establishment of the green belt around the city of Ottawa. The government has now decided to recommend to parliament the necessary measures to make it possible for the crown to acquire ownership of what is known as the green belt around the nation's capital, so as to do what is possible to ensure that the development of the capital area over the long-term future will be in accordance with the national importance and significance of this city. To achieve these ends will require suitable general powers in a bill to establish the national capital commission, as well as to set up the authority over a period of several years for the crown to lend money to the commission to be invested in the purchase of the requisite lands for the purpose.
This project, as the house knows, was considered by a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons two years ago and approved by that committee, with the suggestion that the possibility of achieving this purpose by the use of provincial legislation should be further explored. The government has reached the conclusion that only the acquisition of the land by the crown under the authority of parliament offers any assured hope of achieving this important long-term objective which we believe the committee had in mind.
It has been suggested that the legislature of Ontario might pass legislation to establish this green belt, which would have the effect of taking from private owners of the lands, particularly within the confines of the green belt, the values they could get by developing it for purposes inconsistent with the restrictions necessary to achieve the purposes and aims of setting up the green belt. Such legislation might well give rise to valid arguments that the owners had a legitimate claim for compensation from the province of Ontario because of the effects on them of action taken to accomplish this national purpose. Such problems do not arise under the plan which the government proposes to
place before parliament, under which the crown will buy the property and lease it subject to the restrictions necessary tc accomplish the purpose.
The details concerning the areas to be included in the green belt, the limitations of the use to which lands therein may be put, will be worked out for the approval of the government by the federal district commission after consultation with the local authorities concerned. Broadly speaking, the area and uses will be those placed before the joint committee in 1956. Some modifications will be desirable which have regard to the developments which have occurred since that time. The government wishes to be sure that local views as to the precise details shall be taken into account.
I should like to emphasize that this is a long-term project undertaken in the national interest. It is not a short-term one nor one that has been undertaken at the request of the local municipalities. Experience has shown that unless effectual control is exercised, cities tend to sprawl out into suburbs, resulting in what is called ribbon development, in a manner that is quite contrary to and inconsistent with the long-term planning that is necessary and essential if the capital of Canada is to be preserved and developed so that it will be a capital city of which this generation and succeeding generations can and will be proud.
By investing a reasonable sum now to acquire title to the lands on the boundaries of the city the people of Canada, through parliament, can be assured of that control which is necessary before further developments take place which may indeed result in action being taken too late. During the early years after the land is acquired the rents received for it may not be as much as the interest on the funds borrowed to purchase the lands in question, but the government is confident that over the long-term period the investment will be found to be worth while financially, as well as being necessary to achieve the important purpose which we and the people of Canada as a whole, I believe, have in mind and desire.
I would suggest that the details concerning this matter can best be discussed when the national capital bill is before the house, which I hope will be at a very early date.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED TOLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the St. Lawrence seaway authority of Canada and the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation of the United States in a simultaneous announcement today are making public the proposed tolls which may form the basis of recommendations to their respective governments to meet the 

requirements of the legislation of each country. The recommendations which were submitted by the Canadian tolls committee and by the United States tolls committee are in complete agreement.
The main features of the proposed toll structure are as follows: For each passage through the entire seaway, Montreal to or from lake Erie, a vessel will be assessed 6 cents per gross registered ton of vessel and in addition 42 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 95 cents per ton of general cargo carried. For each passage, Montreal to or from lake Ontario only, a vessel will be assessed 4 cents per gross registered ton of vessel and in addition 40 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 90 cents per ton of general cargo carried.
For partial transit of the new seaway facilities between Montreal and lake Ontario, where there are seven locks, the user will be charged 15 per cent of the applicable toll for each lock transited.
For each passage through the Wellanu canal only a vessel will be assessed 2 cents per gross registered ton of the vessel, and in addition 2 cents per ton of bulk cargo and 5 cents per ton of general cargo carried. In the Welland canal a partial transit will be assessed 50 per cent of the toll irrespective of the number of locks used.
The unit of weight for the collection of tolls on cargo will be a ton of 2,000 pounds.
Commercial vessels carrying passengers will be charged 50 cents per passenger for each lock transited between Montreal and lake Erie in addition to the vessel charge.
The charging of tolls on the Welland canal as part of the seaway in order to defray the capital cost of deepening as well as operating and maintenance expenses is a requirement of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act passed without dissent by the parliament of Canada in 1951. The act pertains to a deep waterway between the port of Montreal and lake Erie.
The suggested tolls, according to the tolls committees, should be sufficient to meet all financial requirements as the anticipated traffic develops. It is believed by the members of the tolls committees that the revenue derived will provide for the annual cost of operation and maintenance of the new seaway facilities and of the Welland canal, and meet interest charges and amortize borrowed moneys over a period covering the next 50 years. They have estimated that in the first year of operation the traffic through the new portion of the seaway would approximate 25 million cargo tons but would rise gradually to 50 million tons by 1968. The latter figure has been used

for the 40 years after the development period, since this is considered to be the workable capacity of the facilities presently existing and under construction between Montreal and lake Erie. For the Welland canal the Canadian committee estimates the tonnage of cargo at 40 million tons in 1959 with a gradual increase to 60 million tons in 1968.
The traffic estimates of the committees anticipate a developmental period extending to 1968, that is a period of 10 years during which there may not be sufficient revenue to meet all the annual financial requirements. However, with the proposed tolls and the level of traffic which is anticipated beginning with the year 1968 they say that the annual revenues will be sufficient to compensate for the deficiencies incurred during the development period, and that all other financial requirements will be taken care of within the period of 50 years.
A simple method of toll collection is proposed based on the necessity of non-interference with prompt passage by any user. Provision is made for prior registration of any vessel and satisfactory security being given for the payment of charges either with the St. Lawrence seaway authority or with the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation, subsequent to which passage will be permitted. Toll collection and invoicing of accounts as well as the preparation of statistical data is proposed to be assigned to the St. Lawrence seaway authority. The St. Lawrence seaway development corporation has agreed to participate and share in the annual cost of these services. Charges will be billed to the owner or agent promptly and will be payable within seven days after the passage of the ship.
For through passage to or from Montreal and lake Ontario, the invoice will show two amounts to be paid: (1) in Canadian funds to cover the proportion applicable to the St. Lawrence seaway authority, which has been determined at 71 per cent of the total charges; and (2) the balance of the account, or 29 per cent, in United States funds, representing the proportion applicable to the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation, payable at any designated bank in Canada or in the United States. Tolls collected for use of the Welland canal will be for the St. Lawrence seaway authority account and payable in Canadian dollars. The committees stated that the division of tolls indicated above is based upon current figures of estimated capital and operating costs, and can be subject to variation as actual costs are determined.
St. Lawrence Seaway-Tolls
The reports stated that the projection of traffic volume and financial requirements has been made, bearing in mind the legislative requirements on the one hand and on the other the desirability of establishing tolls which in the early years will be conducive to the development of traffic. If future events should indicate that traffic conditions or future financial requirements have been either overestimated or underestimated, the necessary adjustments can be made in the toll structure.
Bulk cargo as defined in the proposed tariff will include such commodities as grain and grain products, loose or in sacks, ores and minerals as described, liquids in ships' tanks, pulpwood, poles and logs, woodpulp, waste paper, iron and steel scrap and pig iron. Domestic package freight of each country will also take the bulk cargo rate. All commodities not included in the definition of bulk cargo will be classified as general cargo.
The recommendations of the Canadian tolls committee, together with supporting statistical data, are being made public concurrently.
In accordance with the requirements of their legislation, the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation will hold public hearings at Washington on August 6, 1958, at which interested parties will have an opportunity to express their views on the proposed charges. The St. Lawrence seaway authority, as a matter of policy, will hold public hearings at Ottawa commencing the same day.
Those intending to appear at Ottawa should advise the acting secretary of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, Ottawa, of their intention to make representations, and should also submit 10 copies of their briefs at least 10 days before the date of the hearing.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that hon. members will wish to know the total effect of this levy per bushel of grain or per ton of iron ore, etc. On a cargo of wheat moved from Fort William to Montreal we expect that savings of at least 4 cents a bushel will be realized after allowances for the toll charges. For the movement of iron ore, as there are no published freight rates it is impossible to state the exact saving which will be made. However, the evidence is that the savings through the avoidance of transshipment, and use of large ships, will be far in excess of the levy of 46 cents per ton.
For all the wide range of other commodities that will be carried on the seaway similar savings will be realized, varying with the commodity and the particular conditions of its transport. These include bulk commodities such as coal, pulpwood and petroleum products, package freight-which as

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED TOLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the minister and more particularly, if he will allow me to do so, the St. Lawrence seaway authority for the establishment of a tariff of tolls at this time. When the St. Lawrence seaway authority was established it had two things to do. The first was to build a 27-foot navigation canal from Montreal to lake Erie. The second was to establish a tariff of tolls, the latter being a matter of great importance and one which was extremely complicated.
That is why I would now like to say that I believe the St. Lawrence seaway authority as well as the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation should be commenced for the establishment of that toll in co-operation with each other. I am not in a position, of course, to pass judgment on the matter of tolls; that will require some study, but I would point out to the minister that I am glad he has made this statement because just on Monday of this week my colleagues the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) and the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) complained about the fact that we were being given little or no information concerning the seaway, concerning the imposition of tolls and concerning the manner in which those tolls would be imposed. Now, while we have not been given all the information for which we have asked, we have been given some information and for that I am grateful to the minister.
I would also like to say that as I listened to the information on the various tolls mentioned by the minister, while I am not in a position to comment upon them they did appear to me to be attractive. However, whether they are low enough to be nondiscriminatory to the industries which will be established along the seaway is a matter which will have to be studied by the bodies to which the minister has referred.
As the minister has said, the toll must be high enough to amortize the capital expenditures in connection with the seaway and must be low enough to encourage traffic. Are these tolls low enough to encourage traffic to move freely? I hope they are.
The questions which now come to my mind are, first, will the government seek the
[Mr. Hees.l

approval of the United States government with respect to this tariff of tolls; and second, will the board of transport commissioners hear applications-I now refer to complaints made on Monday by the two hon. members I mentioned previously-with respect to an industry which is being discriminated against? In other words, will the board of transport commissioners have jurisdiction to hear such cases, as outlined in section 15 of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act, or will such cases fall under the jurisdiction of the St. Lawrence seaway authority?
There is one other point which I would like to raise, and this is by way of complaint. I made a complaint on Monday that unfortunately many of the statements which have been emanating from Washington should have emanated from this House of Commons. On at least three different occasions there have been complaints in this house on the part of both the hon. member for Welland and myself that the minister and the government should have given the information to the house and, instead of giving it to the house at the appropriate time, it came from Washington. I am informed on reliable authority that the statement which the hon. minister has just made was given to the press in Washington last night, and that newspapermen in the United States telephoned newspapermen in Canada asking them for their views on the tariff of tolls. The newspapermen in this country had not seen this tariff and were therefore not given an opportunity to consider the tolls. I know this is not the fault of the government but it is certainly the fault of someone, and it is a pretty serious fault because, since the tolls are so complicated, it barely gives our newspapermen a chance to report authoritatively on them.
I would therefore ask the minister why Canadian newsmen did not have the same opportunity as their colleagues in the United States to obtain information on these tolls at least 12 hours before the announcement was made, in order that they might have had an opportunity to prepare their reports.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED TOLLS
speechtext:
I would like to answer the hon. member on that point. It was arranged between the Canadian and United States authorities that this release would be made simultaneously at 2.30 this afternoon. It was my understanding that this release was not to be handed to the press of either country until that time. It was our intention to give this release to the press in Canada simultaneously with my announcement in the house. However, the authorities in the United

States released copies last night, I understand. I was told of that this morning, and was advised that the release bore a release time of 2.30 p.m. today. As soon as I learned that this had been done, which was at about a quarter to twelve this morning, I immediately made arrangements that the statement should be released to the press of Canada at that time for their information with a release time firmly stated upon it of 2.30 this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, we welcome the statement by the minister. A reading of the Congressional Record in the last several months, especially the portions emanating from the House of Representatives, indicates there has been a great deal of misinformation in the United States house as to the part that Canada has played in the seaway and the respective weight of the burdens borne by the two countries, and concerning the whole definition of toll charges.
I hope the government will take the action which seemed to be called for in the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier, and that is to issue an aggressive statement on Canada's position in this whole question of tolls and the role we have played. In other words, the government should do something in the way of a public relations job in the United States and especially in Washington, to let them know the part Canada has played.
I take it from the minister's statement that any possibility of discriminatory clauses against foreign shipping has been completely ruled out. Of course I do not think this is a dead issue, and I hope some of the groups who present briefs to the meeting on August 6 will bring up that matter again, because it is a question that is not completely settled to the satisfaction of many people, especially those along the lake, despite the report of the royal commission on coastal shipping.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to part 1 of this question is yes. In reply to part 2 I would say that

Questions
the following recommendations have been implemented, in whole or in part, by the federal government: 20, 21, 23, 24, 28, 35, 38, 39, 41, 42 and 43. I made a sincere attempt, Mr. Speaker, to prepare, for the information of the hon. gentleman who asked the question and of the house, a short summary of the actual content of those recommendations to which I have referred by number, but I found it was not possible to condense it into a short space. However, if the house would consent I would be prepared to table at this point, so that it may form part of the answer, a written statement showing in detail just what the recommendations were and what has been done in connection with them.

speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
The recommendations that have been implemented, in whole or in part, by the federal government are as follows:
20.	The federal and the provincial governments should give serious consideration, in expanding their systems of penal institutions, to the establishment, on a medium security basis, of such additional institutions as may be required.
Joyceville is being built as a medium security institution and the new Quebec institution will also be of that type.
21.	In the women's prison at Kingston, Ontario, a more intensified system of varied forms of treatment should be instituted.
The commissioner of penitentiaries informs me that additional professional staff has been added.
23.	In relation to the operation of all penal institutions in Canada, more reception centres should be established to which inmates may be initially committed for classification and ultimate committal to the particular institution that provides the most useful form of treatment in their particular cases.
Reception wings have been put in operation in the penitentiaries at Montreal and Prince Albert.
24.	Classification staffs should be provided for all penal institutions in Canada and, where they already exist, they should be increased to an appropriate size.
Classification staffs in the penitentiaries are being increased regularly in size.
28. Every penal institution in Canada should institute an appropriate pre-release program for the benefit of inmates.
Each of the penitentiaries has instituted, by way of experiment, pre-release programs for inmates serving long sentences.
35. As soon as possible, a system of automatic parole review should be instituted for Canada,

thereby dispensing with the present system which requires an application for parole.
The remission service has instituted a system of automatic parole review which is 40 per cent completed.
38.	Some means should be found to provide specialized after-care for particular types of parolees, such as sex offenders, drug addicts, alcoholics and psychopaths.
The remission service, in conjunction with the after-care agencies and with the co-operation of certain clinics, is increasing the amount of specialized after-care that is available for persons of these types.
39.	The federal and provincial governments should increase their financial grants to voluntary aftercare agencies in order to enable them to work more effectively in the correctional field.
There have been annual increases in the amounts that parliament has been asked to appropriate by way of grants to voluntary after-care agencies. The amount for the current fiscal year that is asked is $120,000, divided between the penitentiary service and the remission service.
41.	The annual conference of after-care agencies and government services should be continued in the future.
The conference of after-care agencies has been held annually since the Fauteux report was presented to the government.
42.	A national parole board should be established as recommended in chapter XI of the report.
The speech from the throne forecast a bill to establish a national parole board at the present session of parliament.
43.	The administration of federal correctional services should be organized as suggested in chapter XII of the report.
In partial implementation of this recommendation we have established a committee consisting of the deputy minister of justice, the commissioner of the R.C.M. Police, the commissioner of penitentiaries and the director of the criminal law section of the Department of Justice for the purpose of considering and advising on questions of policy or general concern in connection with matters under our jurisdiction in the correctional field.
The answer to part 3 is no and the answer to part 4 is yes. I should like to state by way of amplification that I answered 3 in the negative because we have not actually commenced the conference, and part 4 in the affirmative because we are taking steps to call that conference this year.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is, of course, in accordance with the rules, a point of order. It is not a debatable motion. It can be transferred for the purpose of debate. Is that at the request of the house or the government? It is not a debatable motion. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

I ask the Prime Minister if he wishes to address himself to this provision of the rule:
All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of "Notices of motions".
Now I raise the question, at whose request will the motion be transferred for debate? If anyone can give me any assistance on the subject I shall be glad to have it. If the Prime Minister or any member has anything to say on that point I would be glad to hear him.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I might point out that reading the first part of rule 47, we find this:
Notices of motions for the production of papers which the member asking for the same intends to move without discussion, shall be marked by him with an asterisk and shall be placed by the Clerk on the order paper under the heading "Notices of motions for the production of papers".
The hon. member has put this question on the order paper marked with an asterisk, yet now he thinks he will get some advantage by changing his mind and having a debate on the subject. I suggest the rule was never intended to enable a member to make such a request.

I should like to submit to Your Honour that on one occasion about two years ago a motion was made by a member of the C.C.F. party for certain documents relating to the Caughnawaga Indian reserve at the time I was minister. I invoked this rule, the motion was transferred, and the government of the day gave an undertaking that there would be an opportunity for debate, which opportunity was provided.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: What does the hon. member say to the point made by the Minister of Public Works, that by placing the notice of motion on the order paper with a star he has elected not to have a debate?

I submit that it is provided in the rules that this transfer can be made. The important word is "transfer". It would have been quite acceptable to me to have no debate if the government had been willing to comply with the motion. Since the Prime Minister has refused the information to the house it does seem to me, sir, that then I can invoke the second part of the standing

Motions for Papers
order and ask to have it transferred for the purpose of having a debate on a matter which, as Your Honour will recall, relates to a document which the Prime Minister gratuitously brought before the house in a previous parliament.

I wonder if I might be heard on the point of order. I want to draw Your Honour's attention to the different language used in the two parts of standing order No. 47. The first part deals with the marking of the question when it is put on the order paper. The second part deals with the transfer when it is called. In other words there are two different points of time, and I think that completely answers the argument made by the Minister of Public Works.
I should like if I may, then, to read the standing order in the light of these remarks. The first part reads:
Notices of motions for the production of papers which the member asking for the same intends to move without discussion, shall be marked by him with an asterisk and shall be placed by the Clerk on the order paper under the heading "Notices of motions for the production of papers".
Then there is a period in the standing order. Then this part comes:
All such notices when called-
And I want to emphasize the words "when called".
-shall be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of "Notices of motions".
In other words, the point I want to make is that two different points of time are envisaged. There is nothing inconsistent in a member placing the motion on the order paper with an asterisk and, when the motion is called, asking for a debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say that it seems to me that this rule is quite clear. It states:
All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion a debate be desired-
It seems to me it is quite clear that it is not the desire of the individual or the member who places the motion on the order paper which is meant, but rather the desire of the house. If the house desires a debate on it, well and good; it will be proceeded with.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not think you can read anything else into this clause except that what is meant is that it is the desire of the house that debate be held.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. If the contention made by the hon. member for Ottawa West is correct, then on every single one of these notices of motions for the production of papers the member who puts that notice on the order paper can force a debate on it.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That would be a ridiculous situation if the house should have to debate every one of these notices of motions simply at the whim of the hon. member who happened to put it on the order paper.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out what I feel would be the practical result of the request made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect to the hon. member may I say that I am not interested in the practical result. I am interested in what this rule means as it reads. If he will address himself to that point of order we shall dispose of it. We all know what the practical result will be.

As to what the rule means, may I say this. The standing order reads in part: All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of "Notices of motions".
I suggest that the hon. member who has made the request, because of the fact that the motion is in his name, is not in order in that request. I suggest further that this rule cannot be applied in order to bring on a debate merely by adopting it because, if we pass it, the motion will go to the bottom of notices of motions and would be No. 46. Those are private members' motions, and it would not come up for debate. Therefore the desired debate would not be achieved. I do not think either, with great respect, that the Prime Minister as such can himself say whether or not a debate may be held. It is up to the house at some future date to decide.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for the assistance he has given me. However, I am still finding some difficulty with this rule. I think it is open to any member to put a notice of motion of this kind on the order paper, under notices of motions, to which heading it will go if it is transferred at this time. As I understand the rule, the marking of the notice with an asterisk simply means that it is dealt with on routine proceedings with other matters that do not require an extensive expenditure of time, and where there is no debate. That is where we find it. If there is a change of mind and a debate is

required on the motion, this rule apparently permits the notice to be transferred to the general heading "Notices of Motions" and, as the hon. member for Assiniboia points out, there it will go to the bottom of the list where it will likely be buried for the rest of the session.
However, I think that was the intention of the rule. The only thing that puzzled me was whether the mover of the motion could in effect change his mind. The question really is whose request or whose desire is to be given effect to. As there has been a request for a debate on this motion, I think effect should be given to that request and that it should be transferred to the order paper under notices of motions.

speechtext:
Having in mind his interest in the humane treatment of animals, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Justice.
In view of newspaper reports to the effect that a certain Ontario chamber of commerce

intends to stage a program of bloodless bullfights for the August 2-4 holiday week end, would the minister inform the house if he considers the present provisions of the Criminal Code stringent enough to prevent any cruelty which might occur as the result of the introduction into Canada of this undesirable and exotic form of entertainment?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CRUELTY TO ANIMALS
speechtext:
I would like to remind the hon. member to consider that he is really asking for a legal opinion, but I do not wish to prevent him from getting such a legal opinion if the minister is prepared to answer his question.
Kon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, I have an answer ready to this question because I appreciate the courtesy of the hon. member in having given me notice. I would, however, point out that I can neither give a firm legal opinion nor do I know what a bloodless bullfight is or might be.
My answer is therefore even more hypothetical in this case than is the hon. member's question. The Criminal Code makes it an offence for a person to wilfully wound or injure cattle, including bulls, and also makes it an offence for a person to wilfully cause or, being the owner, wilfully permit to be caused unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to an animal. It is also an offence for a person in any manner to encourage, aid or assist at the fighting or baiting of animals.
I have seen some of the newspaper reports to which the hon. member has referred, but I do not think it would be proper for me as Minister of Justice to attempt to express in advance any opinion on the question of whether a proposed performance of this kind would or would not contravene the provisions of the Criminal Code to which I have referred. I have no doubt that the local law enforcement authorities will, in accordance with the Canadian tradition in such matters, keep close watch on the situation and will be ready to take appropriate steps at once if, in the course of such a performance, it appears that any violation of the criminal law is involved.

In so far as meals and accommodation are concerned it is felt the availability of these services on an out-patient basis will tend to deter admissions to hospitals. Following your suggestion, I will refrain from getting into that phase of hospital insurance coverage. Needless to say, we are in favour of the principles embodied in the bill, the main part of which appears to me to be the advancement of six months in the application of it and the removal of the restriction which required a certain number of provinces representing a certain portion of the population to have such schemes in operation before any federal participation would take place.

signed agreements and would be covered by July 1, with the added information that other provinces are contemplating establishing plans by way of legislation and that in the immediate future we hope to have another three or four at least, and I hope 10 eventually, participating completely in such a plan.
I think we might ask ourselves this question. Why was it that after the enactment of the legislation which this bill is intended to amend there was a sudden increase in interest on the part of the various provincial governments in instituting hospital insurance plans whereas in prior years some of them, at least so far as public knowledge is concerned, did not appear to be too interested in establishing hospital insurance coverage plans such as the one that has been in effect in my own province for a number of years? I think we can find the answer to that question very easily. The mere fact that the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act was placed on the statute books a few years ago indicated to the provinces that here was a source of financial assistance to them if they wanted to put hospital insurance programs into effect. It acted as a stimulus to those provinces to think in terms of providing provincial schemes. If it were not for the fact that the former Liberal administration introduced such a measure, even though it did not go far enough toward meeting the over-all problem of health care, whereby they would participate with the provinces, some of the provinces that are indicating interest today would probably not have either plans in effect or plans for enacting legislation within the next little while in order to achieve this purpose.
I am sure that it was only because the act was put into effect and the federal government indicated a desire to participate that provincial interest was stimulated to the point where, as the minister indicated, there will be five provinces participating, he hopes, by July 1, and in the not too distant future a number of other provinces, including the province of Quebec which has indicated interest. Therefore in the not too distant future, I hope within a year or two, all ten provinces will get into the picture because of the fact that the act was a stimulus to them. The result will be that we will have fairly uniform, all-inclusive hospital insurance coverage across the nation.
As I said earlier, the principle of the bill is acceptable. It is all right but it is lacking to a great degree. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will refrain from calling me to order for a few minutes and I will try not to say things that will cause you to call me to order. In dealing with the principle of the
Hospital Insurance Act bill I feel I must express our view that the bill is deficient in that, as has been stated by the C.C.F. for many years, it does not go far enough toward providing the type of all-inclusive health coverage that the people of Canada should have and that we should give to them.
Because the present act was a stimulus to a number of provinces to enact legislation providing hospital insurance plans, surely we can expect that if any leadership at all is shown by the government in providing for all-inclusive medical and dental care under the present act there will be an equal stimulus to the provinces to expand their present hospital insurance schemes in order that they will cover medical, dental and other care necessary under an all-inclusive health scheme. In that respect we think there is a great deficiency not only in the bill but in the original act. I can only hope that a Conservative government will be a little more speedy in its acceptance of ideas put forward from this corner of the house than was the former Liberal administration and will not wait until they may think it is politically advantageous to expand the act to provide medical and dental services and an all-inclusive health scheme. I trust that they will do so at the earliest possible moment so that we can provide leadership and stimulate the provinces to expand their schemes. In that way we will not merely be providing hospital insurance coverage or participating in paying bills for people who become ill but will be taking definite corrective measures in the first instance to prevent them from becoming ill and having to go to hospital.
I hope the few remarks I have made will be taken to heart by the minister and government. I know that it will not take place during this session but I hope that between now and the next session of the house the government will undertake a study and provide the necessary leadership in order that we may have an all-inclusive health plan in Canada.

When in 1948 Mr. Mackenzie King introduced his national health program, he pointed out that grants for hospital construction throughout the country were to be considered as the fundamental basis of a national health insurance program. In the years that followed, the former prime minister stated clearly, on more than one occasion, that the Canadian government's policy still consisted in supporting a contributory health insurance plan to be administered by the provinces. This was an excellent formula, one requiring no constitutional amendment, and which allowed the federal government to give financial assistance to provincial administrations, thus respecting provincial autonomy in the fields of public health.
It is a plan financed by all Canadians. The object of the hospital insurance act is to serve the interests of every province. Let us hope that all provinces will avail themselves of the benefits of the act and of the proposed amendment since it would obviously be unfair if the people of one province, who, in the last analysis will be called upon to pay for the plan in operation in another province, cannot enjoy the benefits of this legislation within their own province.
Now, with regard to this act and the proposed amendment, I would like to offer a few remarks about the hospital needs of the province of Quebec. Some years ago, the Quebec deputy minister of social welfare said that about 80 per cent of the citizens of our province cannot afford the costs of a prolonged stay in hospital. About a week ago, a delegation of the hospitals council, made up of 39 institutions, sought financial assistance from the city of Montreal. Dr. Turner, who was heading the delegation, said that the hospital problem is so acute that, unless they get immediate assistance, many hospitals will close down.
We have debts and salaries to pay, he said.
Under the circumstances, the people of the province of Quebec were entitled to expect a more positive and progressive stand on the part of the provincial government.
Since 1955, and 1956 too I believe, we have offered the provinces to join this plan and to get ready for it so as to make it available to the people of our province. Today, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, we are no further ahead than we were at the time. Indeed, I shall quote a statement made by the premier of the province of Quebec, which I think has a bearing on this subject. It is from a Canadian Press report dated October

25, 1955. It shows in a few words how the premier of the province of Quebec feels about this hospital insurance plan. "The premier of the province of Quebec today discounted the possibility of the province joining in a national hospitalization insurance plan. It was stated by the premier that the system of charitable institutions now existing is better adapted to the people of his province."
And there we have the reason why on this 18th day of June 1958, the people in Quebec have no inkling as to when this legislation will apply to their province. I sincerely hope that authorities-busy though they be at the moment patching up certain gas leakage- will manage to find time to allow hospitals to benefit from this hospital insurance plan.
Mr. Speaker, I have therefore shown that this legislation is one of the most beneficial steps taken by the previous Liberal administration and that it meets urgent needs. Accordingly I hope that Quebec authorities will soon take positive steps so that, like other provinces, we might enjoy the benefits of this act. However, even if Quebec authorities do act, I believe that the loss of time of the last two or three years has been so great that, in due course, the provincial government will have to answer for its serious dereliction of duty in this regard.

As the minister indicated, the purpose of this bill is three-fold. It is to bring in basically three amendments, two of which are relatively minor in character and are covered by one section of the bill and a third and more important one dealing with the conditions under which the federal government may begin to share with the provinces in the cost of their hospital insurance schemes.
I may say to the minister that so far as I am concerned little can be said about the first two amendments. As he indicates, the one is clarifying what was really intended and what I think is still implicit in the actual wording of the original measure. With regard to the other, that providing for meals and the like, I think that is a necessary step. I have looked over the section and I still think it could be argued that such provision is included in the present bill; but if the provinces find that it is desirable to have that provision clearly stated, of course there can be no exception taken for the reasons the minister has mentioned. Those who will take advantage of the diagnostic services within the hospital will require to spend some time in a hospital and that procedure will include necessarily, under certain conditions, taking meals in the hospital. Making that provision possible and authorizing the federal government to share in the cost of such provision is one way, as the minister has stated, of avoiding any abuse in the matter of bed occupancy. But with regard to the main amendment, I think that we must give some consideration to the circumstances-again I am not disagreeing with it-and to point out that the fact that this measure is now being introduced confirms the assertion made by hon. members on this side of the house that

The principle involved, he thought, was that insisting on this requirement meant that the federal government was dictating levels of service.
I should be greatly interested in what the minister has to say about that matter because I am fairly familiar with that argument. Is that the only reason why Alberta has not been able to sign the agreement? Or is it because-as I think the minister last night suggested-some examination was still being made of the character of the scheme itself in Alberta? The minister now nods approval, that that is the real reason. I can understand that, although I wonder why that is the case in Alberta. Is it because of the necessary participation, under the Alberta act, of the municipalities in terms of sharing the costs? Or is it because the scheme covers only a percentage of the population of Alberta and consequently does not come within the condition of universal availability, the phrase envisaged in the proposal made by the federal government?
What about British Columbia? British Columbia has had a hospital insurance scheme in being now for a long time. What is the difficulty? What is the attitude taken by the province of British Columbia? The

minister last night, in the report that he gave, did not give us the reasons why British Columbia has not yet signed an agreement. I think the house should be given that information. It may be that arguments have developed which formerly were not thought to be valid but which might on reconsideration be thought to be valid today. I am not saying that is the case. In any event, my curiosity in this matter I think will be understandable when I say that we ought to be informed as to exactly why provinces with schemes now in being have not yet signed agreements with the federal government.
What is the situation with regard to Saskatchewan? That is a province which has had a scheme in being now for some considerable length of time, longer than any other province. It is a province that has acquired considerable know-how and experience with regard to this matter, and one that needs this additional money. Why has no agreement been signed with this province to date? We will be able to judge from the replies given by the minister with respect to the reason why no agreement has thus far been signed and as to what assessment we really should make of the likelihood of an agreement being signed before July 1. It may be that the minister will find very considerable support for the positions he may have had to take with respect to these matters. In any event, as he knows, for some time now I have been asking him in this house, both during the present session and more particularly last fall, as to the reasons why agreements have not been signed and were not signed last fall with any province and only now are they being signed with two provinces.
The same kind of interrogation might be pursued with respect to Manitoba, although the hon. minister says that Manitoba will be coming into the scheme, and I hope that the events of Monday last will not cause any delay in that particular.
I would like to know, for instance, why Prince Edward Island has not been able to come in and why is it that Nova Scotia, while announcing that it will come in by July 1, 1959, has not yet found it possible to sign an agreement? The same is true of the province of New Brunswick, that province having announced that it proposes to begin a scheme on January 1, 1959. Why is it, if that is the case, that that province has also not found it possible to sign an agreement up to the present time?
I do not say this in any critical way, and I hope the minister will not misunderstand me, but I take it that the reason for this amendment being introduced at this time is because the province of Ontario, having
Hospital Insurance Act decided to embark upon a scheme must not be put into the position where, having taken all the necessary steps to implement this huge undertaking in what is the largest province of Canada, it cannot be assured of a contribution being made to the cost of that scheme by the federal government at the starting date of January 1, 1959.
I take it that that is the main reason for this particular legislation, and I do not quarrel with that reason. As I have mentioned on another occasion, I indicated to Premier Frost in the spring of 1957 that if six provinces had not complied with the terms of section 2 of the main act, we would by the end of September have taken steps to make it possible to pay our share to Ontario as well to other consenting provinces in a manner different from that provided by section 2 of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. I think therefore it is a fair argument-as has already been suggested-that if the government had pursued this matter with vigour last fall, and if it had really urged the provinces as it is apparently now doing to sign these agreements, it would not have been necessary to bring forward this legislation. Instead of having six provinces sign this agreement by July 1, 1958, we would perhaps have had the actual signatures of two other provinces thereby making this scheme more nation-wide in scope than will now be the case. To show that this is not mere fancy, I would like to turn to what I said in this house on October 17 last, when we were discussing inter alia the matter of interim supply. I quote from page 81 in volume 1 of Hansard of that date, when in addressing the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) I said as follows:
Now, we are surely entitled to know whether any progress at all has been made in this matter. The province of Ontario has indicated that it proposes to implement its scheme on January 1, 1959, and when I last conferred with them in my own capacity as Minister of National Health and Welfare I was informed by the premier of Ontario that not later than the end of September he should be in a position to know definitely whether or not the federal government would be able, pursuant to the act, to provide the government of Ontario with its share of the cost of the operation of the Ontario scheme.
Unless some progress has been made I am afraid this situation is not calculated to give much encouragement. If Ontario is going to begin its scheme on January 1, 1959, unless it is to bear the full cost itself it must immediately know whether the other five consenting provinces will have conformed to the requirements of the hospital insurance act, since that legislation provides that the federal money shall be paid only when these six consenting provinces have schemes in being and in support of which the proclamation of the measures under which they operate has taken place. In other words their legislation must be in force and their scheme must be in force.

Hospital Insurance Act
And then later on I said-and this is significant:
If no agreements have been signed, well then, it is clear that Ontario's position, in so far as the starting date announced by the premier is concerned, is in great jeopardy unless the minister is prepared at some later date to suggest to this committee that there should be an amendment to the act to provide for payments on a basis not now envisaged by the hospital insurance act itself.
I think that clearly indicates and confirms the situation which I have just pictured. The reason for this legislation is, quite properly, in order not to embarrass the province of Ontario which has taken such steps. This legislation has become necessary but could have been avoided if this government had taken vigorous steps during last summer and fall to bring about the signing of an agreement with the six provinces which had consented prior to the election of June 1957 to the scheme introduced by the previous administration.
There is another point which I think should be made by those of us who are on this side of the house. That is with respect to those provinces which will now be the beneficiaries of this particular amendment. If it is justified for this government to now pay out money to the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia, how does the minister justify not having paid moneys out to Saskatchewan, to British Columbia and to Alberta long before this? By what principle does this government arrive at this particular type of payment to these provinces? It could be argued, in so far as the last administration is concerned, that payments were conditional upon the existence of six schemes being in force, but that condition does not appear in the present amendment. So how does the minister justify not having paid out this money in advance of this situation which has developed to those three provinces which had schemes in being long before July 1, 1958?
It is not for me to champion the cause of these three provinces, none of which is my own province, but as a citizen of Canada I believe we have a right to expect that all provinces will be treated on the same basis of principle and equity and I suggest that having refused to take this position from June 25, 1957 until the present time it will now be very difficult for the administration to explain to the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan why it is now taking steps to provide for a sharing of costs by the federal government only as of July 1, 1958.
The minister does not find this to his liking, and possibly when he replies he will indicate exactly what he means when he expresses disagreement with my point of view. If I am


wrong, I would like to be told, but I am sure that is a perfectly defensible position and hon. gentlemen opposite who were on this side of the house argued that the existing provision in the act was not fair to those provinces which had schemes then in being. If it was unfair a year and a half ago surely under circumstances that are much less restrictive it would be difficult not to argue that the provinces of Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Alberta should have been reimbursed by the administration long before this.
The minister was good enough to table the agreement made with Newfoundland and the one made with Ontario. He will recall that when he announced the agreement with Newfoundland I asked him in this house whether or not the agreement with Newfoundland was on the same terms as that with the province of Ontario and the minister's reply was that both agreements were under the act. That was not my question as I indicated by my comment which went unnoticed and uncommented upon by the minister. I do find that the agreements are not the same. It is not that I am criticizing the differences in the agreements but I think it should be pointed out, as was remarked upon by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Vivian) and the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan)-and quite properly so-that the two agreements do not provide exactly the same benefits in the case of Ontario and Newfoundland. There is no quarrel in so far as the federal government is concerned. It is up to each province to decide the extent to which it wishes to take advantage of the federal legislation and I am not criticizing my hon. friend but it is interesting to point out that in the case of Ontario the province only accepts the diagnostic services program to the extent of in-patients and with regard to emergency cases in the category of out-patients.

speechtext: Order. I must remind hon. members that we are currently discussing a bill which has nothing to do with federal-provincial relations between the federal government at Ottawa and the province of Quebec. To put the point absolutely in its true perspective, may I say that I believe the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) should adhere in his speech to the matter being discussed which is the bill he has in front of him. I believe also that the same applied to the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) who in his speech undoubtedly concentrated more on federal-provincial relations between the government of Canada and the province of Quebec than he did on the bill. Therefore may I ask hon. members to discuss the bill under debate at present and leave federal-provincial relations in their proper sphere.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for having given this opinion because I am sure if this matter had not been raised before by

our Liberal friends we would not have had any discussion of the provincial government. 1 am going to continue in English, Mr. Speaker, because I wish to be understood very clearly on this question by my friends from the other provinces and those from the province of Quebec. If I get up to speak on this question it is because I want to say to the minister that I am completely agreeable to a scheme of health insurance in Canada. However, I notice in the bill an implication of the law concerning that part of the bill which states that drugs supplied shall be administered in the hospital. I know that it never entered the minister's mind to cause the people to have any doubts concerning pharmacists. As a pharmacist, I should say we enjoy a very good standing in society. As a result of the amendment in this bill, there may be some people who would question the equity of it in relation to pharmacists.
We are authorized to distribute prescription drugs, pharmaceuticals and biologicals. It is for this reason I am speaking on this question. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that many of the patients who would benefit from this insurance plan are people who may sometimes have to leave the hospital for a period of convalescence or for other reasons. Perhaps these people would need drugs and certain substances in the treatment of their condition. At the moment these persons would have to go back to the hospital in order to obtain these drugs from the hospital itself instead of being able to procure them from the pharmacist.
While I agree with the general principle of the bill, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister that, in this particular respect, the bill may cause certain disagreements between the pharmaceutical profession and others in connection with the administration of these drugs. It is for this reason I have intervened in the debate, and I hope my observations will be given consideration.

There have been many suggestions made during the course of this debate this afternoon, all of which I am very pleased to hear. Of course, I would point out that I have to disagree with some of the comments that have been made. The hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque) indicated that he hoped there would be more than two provinces that would have signed by July 1. I think it was this member who indicated that a salesman does not feel he has closed a deal until he has a signature on the dotted line. I quite understand that approach. I would assure him, however, as I did earlier that I have every expectation there will be five provinces that will have signed by that date.
There were several speakers from the official opposition who took great pleasure in giving some credit for this legislation to the former government. I have no hesitation in agreeing that it was the former government that brought this legislation into force in April, 1957. I would point out, however, and I have mentioned this previously, that it is my firm belief that if the old government had been returned to power the federal government would not be participating in hospital insurance in any province in Canada until January 1, 1959.

under section 1, which deals with subparagraph (iv) of paragraph (f) of section 2 of the act having to do with the provision of drugs, I should like to know what is meant there by "when administered in the hospital". If a patient is brought in, for instance, for an X-ray, is he considered to be an in-patient while he is there, just while the X-ray is being taken? Then, in connection with certain diagnostic services, a person may come to the hospital just for X-ray diagnostic services. Such patients are often given dyes which are ordinarily supplied by the hospital and which must be taken at regular intervals outside. If the hospital supplied those particular dyes for the patient to take, would it be covered under this act?

and the minister cannot be charged with any action taken by any provincial government. However, the question is this. Does Ontario take full advantage of the diagnostic services proposal? I submit that the minister is wrong in saying that it does so.

The whole series of diagnostic services that are contemplated in the case of out-patients providing for people who do not go to hospital at all, such as provisions for the use of those modern instruments used by the medical profession to give good diagnosis, are not being accepted by Ontario in so far as this agreement is concerned.

speechtext: I would like to pursue that a little further, particularly in view of the fact that this act provides for an agreement between the federal and provincial governments in so far as hospital insurance is concerned.

I know it is. I have known of cases where the wives and dependants of service men who have served in Europe for some time, those wives and dependants having been born in British Columbia, upon their return to Canada have been deprived of hospital insurance owing to the present regulations in that province, namely, the one year residence requirement. This has proved to be of great expense to them, and I know of one case where a man incurred on behalf of his family some $1800 in hospital expenses shortly after he returned home. I know of another case where a wife was taken ill and there were expenses of $500 or $600.
It seems to me that when these men are engaged in the defence of this country and are sent overseas and their wives go with them there should be a federal responsibility. They are defending this country and performing a service for the whole of Canada, and it seems to me that under the new arrangements these wives and dependants who are returning from overseas will still be denied the immediate benefits of hospital insurance under this act, which is in effect in the province to which they will return. I would therefore ask the minister, in view of the fact that the federal government is responsible for the welfare of the forces and their
(Mr. Monteith (Perth).]

dependants and also of veterans, would it not be possible to have some clause written into the agreement between the provinces and the federal government providing for the serviceman's wife and his dependants receiving hospital insurance and diagnostic services immediately on their return to the province from which they left to proceed overseas?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext: Does the minister think it fair that servicemen who have volunteered to serve their country and who are removed from the country should be penalized on that account with respect to their wives and dependants when they return to their home province, and be denied the benefits of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act for a period of three months?
